name: Weight-loss jabs (GLP-1) for face leaning

lead: GLP-1 weight-loss injections such as semaglutide lower appetite and body weight, and some people in looksmaxxing and aesthetic circles use them to get a leaner, more defined face where bone structure shows.

The chain is fat loss: the drugs mimic the gut hormone GLP-1, reducing appetite and slowing gastric emptying, and as body fat falls, facial fat falls with it. In a phase III trial of 1,961 adults with obesity, mean weight change at 68 weeks was about -14.9% with semaglutide versus -2.4% with placebo. Face leaning is a by-product of general weight loss; no drug in this class is approved for reducing facial fat. Recent reviews discuss 'Ozempic face', the hollow or aged look that can follow rapid fat loss.

paras: These are prescription injectables used over months, usually with diet and exercise changes. People who want a leaner face typically watch the pace of loss and pair it with strength training to keep muscle.

Common effects include nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea; gallstones and a boxed thyroid-tumour warning (from rodent studies) are listed. They are prescription-only, and the FDA says compounded forms have not been shown safe or effective.

angle.text: GLP-1 jabs cut appetite, body fat falls, and the face slims so bone structure shows. Trials measured body weight rather than faces, and rapid loss can also bring the hollowing popularly called 'Ozempic face'.

lead: Weight-loss jabs are injectable GLP-1 receptor agonist medicines, such as semaglutide (sold as Ozempic and Wegovy), that reduce appetite and body weight. In looksmaxxing and aesthetic-medicine discussion they are sometimes described as a way to lose facial fat and obtain a leaner, more defined face, and the downside of rapid facial fat loss is popularly called "Ozempic face."[1][2]

Semaglutide was approved in the US for type 2 diabetes in December 2017 and, at a higher dose, for weight management in June 2021. In a phase III trial of 1,961 adults with obesity, mean weight change at 68 weeks was about -14.9% with semaglutide versus -2.4% with placebo.[1] Face leaning is a side effect of general weight loss rather than a targeted effect; no drug in this class is approved for reducing facial fat.

Published clinical literature on the face specifically is mostly recent narrative reviews and surgeon commentaries rather than controlled trials. Several 2026 papers discuss whether "Ozempic face" is a distinct clinical entity and how rapid weight loss affects facial ageing.[3]

paras: Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article lists GLP-1 drugs among substances discussed in the community, noting that people without a medical indication may obtain them through a grey market of unregulated products, and lists stomach, pancreas and gallbladder problems among the risks.[2]

Proponents of using them for the face argue that facial fat reduction sharpens the jawline and cheekbones and that fat loss is a common first step to a more defined appearance. Aesthetic clinicians and surgeons describe the same fat loss as a possible cause of hollowing, skin laxity and an older look, particularly in people who lose weight rapidly.[3]

sections.h: Facial changes with rapid weight loss
paras: The term "Ozempic face" emerged in popular media in the early 2020s as semaglutide prescribing grew. Recent literature includes a systematic review by Daneshgaran and colleagues and commentary in Aesthetic Surgery Journal Open Forum questioning whether it is a construct, a consequence or a clinical entity, and clinical-dermatology and cosmetic-dermatology papers on mechanisms of facial ageing with these drugs.[3]

Reviews generally attribute the appearance to loss of facial fat pads and skin elasticity associated with weight loss in general, which is also seen after bariatric surgery and other rapid weight loss, rather than to a drug-specific effect; this remains under discussion.[3]

Common effects are nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting, constipation and abdominal pain, typically peaking during dose escalation. Gallstones are a recognised risk, and the US label carries a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumours based on rodent studies.[1]

A 2024 systematic review cited by Wikipedia found lean mass loss varied between studies, from negligible to substantial, while the ratio of lean to total mass rose; a 2025 review found people regain on average about two thirds of lost weight within a year of stopping.[1]

The FDA declared shortages of Ozempic and Wegovy from August 2022, and compounding pharmacies prepared versions under the shortage rules. The FDA states that compounded semaglutide salt forms have not been shown to be safe or effective and that it does not evaluate compounded drugs.[1]

Trials of semaglutide measured body weight and metabolic outcomes, not facial appearance: the March 2021 phase III trial in 1,961 adults reported -14.9% versus -2.4% body weight at week 68.[1] No controlled trial has measured facial fat or attractiveness as an outcome; facial effects appear only in reviews and case-based commentary.[3]
